findings: A: refuted - the standard reading stops at 100 mm in a 130 mm bed, and only the eleven cores went deeper
B: refuted - 'raised to a collar' fixes one drop height; cross-arena comparison presupposes a standard drop
D: refuted - exact inversion of Pallenmoor's quoted comparison
justification: A dies on 'how many blows take it to a hundred millimetres' set against 'The floor is 130 millimetres of washed silica sand': the standard reading stops 30 mm short of the bottom, and the only work that reached the bottom was coring 'in eleven places', not at each of the thirty grid points. B dies on 'a ring weight raised to a collar and let fall' - a collar is a fixed stop, so the drop height is standardised, and the article's whole comparative apparatus ('the same pair of grids from a hundred and forty other arenas') presupposes that it is. D dies on the exact reversal of 'The gap between my February morning and my July afternoon is still wider than the gap between this school and any other school I test.' Key C is verbatim: 'in the cold the first blow took the cone two-thirds as deep, and the count nearly doubled.'

findings: A: refuted - bottom wax was in better condition than top wax
B: refuted - sieved grains matched the original specification
C: refuted - the unturned 80 mm is the hard layer, explicitly under nine years of hoofprints
justification: A dies on 'the wax he brought up from the bottom was in better condition than the wax at the top'. B dies on 'the grains he sieved came out much as the original specification had them'. C dies on 'Eighty millimetres of it had not been turned since the day it was laid, and under nine years of hoofprints it had gone firm enough to lean a spade on' - the unturned depth is the hard layer, not a loose one, and it is expressly under the hoofprints, not out of their reach. Key D rests on 'about 8 per cent by weight' in the top 50 millimetres against 'nearer 3' below.

findings: A: refuted - 'whatever their age', and some of the stable arenas are older
C: refuted - those floors are 'plain sand and fibre', i.e. unwaxed
D: refuted - 'the same pair of grids' fixes an identical protocol across arenas
justification: A dies on 'The waxed ones move, whatever their age' together with 'some of them older than this one' - age is the variable the text explicitly excludes. C dies on 'In the schools laid on plain sand and fibre', which leaves them no wax at all, and on the thresholds that make any wax temperature-sensitive. D dies on 'the same pair of grids' and 'the morning grid and the afternoon grid', which fix the reading hours as identical across arenas. Key B is the contrast the paragraph draws and the next one names: 'The wax is a paraffin blend, and it is doing most of that work.'

findings: A: key - 'the care is the most useful thing about him'
B: refuted - 'changed one thing and left the other alone'; a tine setting cannot answer a question with 'no horse above the cone'
C: refuted - the instrument confirms the riders rather than discounting them
D: refuted - exact reversal of 'it is worth more than they are'
justification: B dies on 'The yard has changed one thing and left the other alone' together with 'The tester measures a surface; there is no horse above the cone': the tine change answers the layering finding, the heaters were 'costed and not ordered', and the piece closes on a thermometer reading four - nothing there is offered as an answer to soundness. C dies on 'Both figures moved, and they moved together', and on wax thresholds that reproduce the riders' January/July complaint exactly, so their report is vindicated rather than psychologised. D dies on the exact reversal of 'That is a good deal less than the trade's brochures offer, and it is worth more than they are.' Key A sits on 'Here Pallenmoor is careful, and the care is the most useful thing about him.'

findings: A: refuted - bottom wax better, sand 'hardly changed'; the unturned depth is not being worn out
B: refuted - heating controls only the cold end; 'above about twenty-five it goes slack' leaves the July condition untouched
D: refuted - 'The temperature is doing more in that room than the tractor is'
justification: A dies on 'the wax he brought up from the bottom was in better condition than the wax at the top' plus 'The sand itself had hardly changed' - nothing down there is wearing out. B dies on 'Above about twenty-five it goes slack, the grains slide past one another, and the floor gets deep' read against 'deep and tiring by a July afternoon': warming controls only the cold end, so a school kept warm still meets the July condition, and 'I can't put a number on it; these readings won't carry one' blocks the quantitative counterfactual outright. D dies on 'The temperature is doing more in that room than the tractor is.' Key C names both mechanisms the third paragraph builds and the last paragraph acts on.

findings: A ('Hence'): refuted - 'Ending is the harder half' denies that the ending follows from the start
B ('Rather'): refuted - 'again' is additive; the first claim is affirmed, not corrected
D ('Elsewhere'): refuted - 'five seconds later' keeps the same hall and event
justification: A ('Hence') dies on 'Ending is the harder half': the ending's unanimity is a separate problem with its own mechanism, not a consequence of the synchronised start, and 'and again there has been no signal' marks parallelism rather than result. B ('Rather') dies on that same 'again' - nothing in the preceding sentence is being corrected, and its claim is upheld ('A hall organises itself in about a fifth of a second'). D ('Elsewhere') dies on 'five seconds later the sound stops': same room, same event, a later moment, not another place. Key C is the additive-parallel connective the two halves require.

findings: B ('cut in'): refuted - interruption sense; the stated risk is non-participation
C ('fall in'): refuted - bare 'fall in' is form up / collapse, with no participation sense
D ('break in'): refuted - same interruption sense as B
justification: B ('cut in') and D ('break in') both carry the interruption sense and die on what the sentence says the risk is: 'for the length of one clap you are alone with an opinion nobody asked for' - the failure mode is that the others do not participate, not that they cut across you. C ('fall in') has no participation reading without a complement; bare 'fall in' means to form up or to collapse, whereas the paragraph is explicitly about joining ('the second pair of hands matters more than the first: it turns a private view into a public event'). Key A is the collocation that sense requires.

findings: A ('transaction'): refuted - takes no 'about + question' complement and nothing is exchanged
C ('bargain'): refuted - outcome noun against 'conducted' and against 'the coming-down is a ___'
D ('settlement'): refuted - same outcome-noun failure
justification: A ('transaction') dies on the complement 'about how long is decent' - a transaction is an exchange, not a process about a question, and no value changes hands here. C ('bargain') and D ('settlement') are outcome nouns and die on 'conducted at speed and without words' together with the frame 'the coming-down is a ___': the gap names the process itself, not the result it arrives at. Key B takes 'about', takes 'conducted', and is exactly the wordless high-speed mutual adjustment the sentence describes.

findings: A ('rehearsed'): refuted - 'No one has agreed to anything, there is no conductor to watch'
B ('outspoken'): refuted - a speech word for applause the text calls 'without words', and no concessive tension
C ('brief'): refuted - collapses the 'Although' into agreement with 'not permitted to run long'
justification: A ('rehearsed') dies on 'No one has agreed to anything, there is no conductor to watch' and on 'not one of the people in it could explain how' - the passage's governing claim is that none of this is prepared. B ('outspoken') is a speech word applied to applause the text insists is 'conducted at speed and without words', and it puts no strain on the concessive. C ('brief') is the trap for a reader who takes only the main clause: it makes the 'Although' clause agree with 'it is not permitted to run long' (and with 'Four or five seconds'), leaving the concession nothing to concede. Key D supplies the tension 'Although' needs - warm, and capped even so.

findings: A ('narrowly'): refuted - no manner reading for giving applause
C ('instinctively'): refuted - 'A room asked for a big hand' is prompted, and the sound must differ audibly
D ('eagerly'): refuted - eager applause would not be audibly lesser than the recorder player's
justification: A ('narrowly') has no available manner reading for giving a round of applause. C ('instinctively') dies twice: on 'A room asked for a big hand for a stranger', since prompted applause is by definition not instinctive, and on 'everybody present can hear that it is not the same sound the recorder player got', which requires an adverb that degrades the sound rather than one that matches the passage's spontaneity theme. D ('eagerly') dies on that same clause from the other side - eager applause would be at least as warm as the wholehearted kind, not audibly different from it. Key B is the obligation reading the asked-for/spontaneous contrast demands.

findings: A: refuted - 'The loop runs at the speed it always has'
B: refuted - 'Nothing shows on the ward; the colour comes with the spinning'
C: refuted - 'Blood gases have never gone by tube; a porter walks those down'
justification: A dies on 'The loop runs at the speed it always has' - the halved rejects follow the two foam-lined bins, not any slowing. B dies on 'Nothing shows on the ward; the colour comes with the spinning'. C dies on 'Blood gases have never gone by tube; a porter walks those down', which is also the option most likely to be affirmed from outside knowledge. Key D is her own line, 'It's the stop at the far end that does it', which is what the stem's attribution to Ashvenor requires.

findings: A: refuted - the plan was enclosed by the neighbour's attorney, not Ruddiforth's
B: refuted - the bank was maintained ('cut from above ... cleaned from below'); the trigger is the October survey
C: refuted - 'The previous October ... had chained and pegged' places the survey before the November claim
justification: A dies on 'The neighbour's attorney enclosed a tracing of the railway company's deposited plan' - the plan came from the other side of the quarrel. B dies on 'cut from above by one and cleaned from below by the other', which describes a hedge under continuing joint maintenance, and on the sequence: the claim follows the pegging, while 'both sides agree the thorn was last laid in 1839' is stated as common ground, not a grievance. C dies on 'The previous October a surveyor had chained and pegged the line', whose 'previous' plus pluperfect place the survey before the November 1845 claim (and an October after the letters would fall after the scheme was given up). Key D follows from the landmark pairing 'An ash grew in the stone gap; a culvert ran under the lane' laid across 'from the stone gap down to the lane' and 'from the ash to the culvert'.

findings: B: refuted - 'Ett svepskäl är det inte. Kostnaden är verklig'
C: refuted - 'Fler särskilda kvällar begär jag inte' and 'Att ensemblen vänjer sig ... kan jag inte lova'
D: refuted - she has no proposal for lilla scenen and asks for stora scenen from next season
justification: B dies on 'Ett svepskäl är det inte. Kostnaden är verklig och ska räknas med' - she signs on to the ensemble's objection rather than dismissing it. C dies on 'Fler särskilda kvällar begär jag inte. Fyra kan bli sex och sedan åtta' and on 'Att ensemblen vänjer sig vid remsan kan jag inte lova', which removes habituation as any kind of pacing premise. D dies on 'Om lilla scenen kan bära samma sak vet jag inte ... och något förslag för den scenen har jag inte', and reverses her order of operations. Key A carries both halves of her position: 'texten [bör] gå på varje föreställning på stora scenen' while conceding that 'den som vet att remsan går spelar inte som förut'.

findings: A: refuted - 'Raden rymmer fyra kvällar'; åtta is a growth she refuses
B: refuted - the every-spread footer is 'Slingans symbol', not the row
C: refuted - the technician is listed 'Längre bak i programbladet' under a separate heading
D: key - verbatim 'inklämd mellan syntolkning och skolföreställningar'
justification: A dies on 'Raden rymmer fyra kvällar'; the eight belongs to a hypothetical escalation she explicitly rejects ('Fyra kan bli sex och sedan åtta ... Fler särskilda kvällar begär jag inte'). B dies on 'Slingans symbol finns längst ned på varje uppslag i programbladet' - the repeated footer is the loop's symbol, while the row has one fixed slot in the höstprogram. C dies on 'Längre bak i programbladet står Ingegerd Hörnfeldt under rubriken Text och teknik' - the technician is named elsewhere, not on the row. Key D is the opening clause verbatim, and no other option is true of the row anywhere in the text.

findings: B: refuted - 'mot det hjälper varken broddar eller lättare lass'
C: refuted - loads went by hand-drawn kälke; skis explicitly could not pull
D: refuted - the skare is 'inte hal om morgonen' and turns blank only later in the day
justification: B dies on 'och mot det hjälper varken broddar eller lättare lass'. C dies on 'Lassen gick på kälke i stället, och kälken drogs för hand' together with 'Skidor dög till att ta sig fram med, men inte till att dra med' - skis moved people, they did not take over the horse's pulling. D dies on 'Skaren är inte hal om morgonen. Den är sträv som fint grus under sulan, och blank blir den först fram på dagen', by which hour the travelling is over. Key A is 'Skaren som bar en karl gick sönder under hoven'.

findings: A: refuted - 'Var gård körde för sig, och sällan väntade någon in grannen'
B: key - 'Veckorna kom när de kom' / 'bestämde sig kvällen innan'
C: refuted - the window is four to ten in the morning, repeated over weeks
D: refuted - 'en väg som inte finns resten av året'
justification: A dies on 'Var gård körde för sig, och sällan väntade någon in grannen'. C dies on 'Man ger sig i väg vid fyra, i mörker, och vid tio är det över' plus 'Bärigheten varar några timmar' - the window is a morning of a few hours recurring over weeks, not one long night. D dies on 'Vi gick tvärs över sjön mot Olivia Sjödins lada, en väg som inte finns resten av året', reinforced by 'under de timmarna räknas varken diken eller gärdsgårdar'. Key B rests on 'Veckorna kom när de kom' and 'Man såg på himlen och bestämde sig kvällen innan'.
